newsitem.title: USA: School spending tops Michigan governor's budget.
newsitem.headline: School spending tops Michigan governor's budget.

text.p: Michigan Gov. John Engler unveiled an $8.5 billion general fund budget for fiscal 1998 on Thursday that places school funding at the top of his spending list.
"Spending on K-12 education will exceed spending for everything else in the general fund budget combined," Engler said in a news release.
Engler's budget calls for a $541 million increase in state spending on schools that would boost entire school aid spending in the $30.9 billion all-funds budget to $9.1 billion.
Much of the increase would be applied to the state's foundation grant, which would rise by 2.6 percent to $5,445 per pupil in the coming fiscal year.
Engler said the boost in per pupil funding would bring "greater equity to school spending."
The proposed budget contains no contigency should the state ultimately lose a funding lawsuit brough by 84 school districts, according to state budget director Mark Murray.

In November, the Michigan Supreme Court agreed to hear an appeal of a September 1995 appellate court ruling that the state had not been meeting its constitutional requirement of funding its share of total education costs, particularly in the special and driver's education areas. If upheld on appeal, 16-year-old lawsuit could cost the state $500 million.
"We still believe we have solid legal ground," Murray said, adding that oral arguments in the appeal are scheduled for April.

The governor's budget also allocates about $10 million to offset the costs to school districts, community colleges and libraries of so-called Renaissance Zones. In December, 11 zones throughout the state were chosen to be virtually free of most state and local taxes.
On the capital expenditure side, Engler proposed $70 million for a new justice center in Lansing that would be financed with lease revenue bonds.

Murray said the legislature needs to increase the state building authority's bond cap by $700 million to accomodate the new bonding proposal, as well as about $700 million of bond-financed projects approved by lawmakers in December.

Engler's budget projects a $200,000 balance on Sept. 30, 1998. Murray said that no deposits to the state's rainy day fund, which currently stands at $1.1 billion, are anticipated in the coming fiscal year. However, if any surpluses do occur, that money would be placed in the fund, he added.

Murray characterized the governor's spending plan as a solid, but tight budget that does not include any further tax cuts. Tax cuts enacted over the past few years are expected total $2 billion in fiscal 1998, according to budget documents.
